title: Stage fright and dissatisfaction with his recordings
summary: He never lost his fright of audiences, feels insecure when soloing even in recording, and never kept his own records.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Oh yes, yeah, it showed inside. Yeah, I never could -- I was never at ease, and I've never been satisfied with anything I played since.
Because of not feeling at ease?
How about when there isn't an audience?
Oh, I can do anything I want when nobody's there. But the minute you see that -- those people out there, then something happens.
How about in recording? When there's only your fellow musicians and no real audience.

It's all right. Everything is all right then until I have to solo, and immediately the feeling of insecurity sets in. And I begin to become a little confused as to what I want to play, and how I want one thing to follow another.
You always come through sounding so

Well, I don't know how to explain that. In fact, recording I've always been a little confused anyway because in my efforts, tonal wise, I've always tried to emphasize the open tone -- the "oo" sound. And in recording, the "e" sound is very important. It cuts through so that it relaxes that monotonous oo-ness on records.
Uh-huh. So are you satisfied -- or are you saying you're not satisfied with your recordings?

Well, I'm not satisfied. I've never been satisfied. That is probably why that until today, I have very, very -- in fact, I never even collected a record. I would -- I didn't want any. I didn't want to hear that again. So I don't --
So you don't have your own records?
I don't have any records. Since I've been out of music, I've had several of them given to me. But they're home on the shelf. I don't play them. I don't even have a record player.
